slides.title: Brand Archetypes as a System
slides.subtitle: The constraint that makes every downstream decision decidable.

slides.title: They did not run out of money. They changed what was working.
slides.lead: Tropicana. Gap. Coca-Cola in 1985. The most public brand failures are almost never product failures.
bullets: They changed the orange on the carton, the typeface on the logo, the formula in the bottle — and customers who had been buying without thinking for twenty years suddenly stopped.
"Don't change what's working" sounds easy. It isn't, because **nobody in the room understands what is actually working.**
What they cannot see is the *recognition asset*: the accumulated pattern of touchpoints that lets a customer's eye snap to your product on a crowded shelf at 8 AM without engaging conscious thought.
That asset is invisible until it is destroyed. And it is destroyed, specifically, by archetype drift.

slides.title: "Archetype" is doing four different jobs
slides.lead: The confusion between them will cost you, so let me separate them once.
bullets: **Jungian psychological archetypes** — the Mother, the Shadow, the Trickster. Claims about human psychology. Jung was not building a brand strategy framework.
**Personality typology** — the Myers-Briggs descendants. Claims about individual people.
**Genre archetypes** — the Reluctant Hero, the Wise Mentor. Claims about storytelling.

**Brand archetypes** — the twelve-archetype system formalized by Mark and Pearson in *The Hero and the Outlaw* (2001). Claims about how brands organize identity and how customers form recognition. That is this chapter.

slides.title: Every archetype carries its own failure mode
slides.lead: Inner ring: the identity. Outer ring: its shadow — what that identity becomes when its commitments curdle.
slides.why: the chapter lists all twelve, each with 'its core motivation and its shadow', and says 'the shadow matters as much as the archetype' — a genuine two-level taxonomy; Innocent and Everyman are accented because all three drift cases sit there

slides.title: Read the motivation. Not the dictionary definition.
slides.lead: The names will mislead you if you take them literally.
bullets: **Hero** does not mean your brand is noble. It means your brand is organized around the idea that its customer can become better through effort. *The customer is the hero. The brand is the equipment.*
**Outlaw** does not mean illegal or antisocial. Harley-Davidson's customers are accountants and lawyers who want, for the weekend, to feel like they stepped outside the system.
**Caregiver** does not mean soft or low-status. Johnson & Johnson's whole line — baby powder, bandages, surgical instruments — says *we protect the ones who cannot protect themselves.*
The shadow is useful to you in exactly one way: **it tells you where to watch.** When you pick an archetype, you also pick your most likely failure mode.

slides.title: Thirty days of small decisions
slides.lead: You have just launched a tool. Someone has to decide the tagline, the doc tone, the sponsorship, the button colour, the founder's headshot, the error message.
slides.why: chapter runs both branches from the same thirty days: without an archetype 'each decision is made in isolation … a brand that looks like it was designed by a committee that never met'; with one, 'each decision has a constraint'

slides.title: The cheapest consistency device you can buy
slides.lead: A customer does not experience your brand once. They experience it hundreds of times — a tweet, a search result, a friend's recommendation, a push notification, a package on a shelf.
bullets: Each experience is a data point. If the data points are consistent, the customer builds a **model** of who the brand is. That model is the recognition asset.
If they are inconsistent, the model never forms. The customer has met your brand before and cannot place you.
The archetype is the cheapest instrument for enforcing consistency because **it operates at the level of identity rather than execution**.

You do not tell every designer, writer and engineer what to produce. You tell them who the brand is. A designer who knows the brand is a Sage makes different choices than one who knows it is a Jester — consistently, without a style guide.

slides.title: The strength, taken too far, is the failure
slides.lead: The shadow is structurally related to the archetype's strength. That is the part that took me a while to see clearly.
bullets: The Innocent's strength is purity. **The shadow of purity is denial** — refusing bad news, messaging that reads as willfully naive, out of touch with anything complicated or dark.
The Sage's strength is expertise. The shadow of expertise is dogmatism — certain, preachy, unable to update when the evidence changes.
The Hero's shadow is contempt for people who have not become better. It sneers at users who struggle.
The Caregiver's shadow is martyrdom: *we sacrifice for you, and you should notice that.*

slides.title: Shadow drift, or category error?
slides.lead: The analytical frame has four elements; this is the one that classifies the failure. The chapter names Tropicana and New Coke outright. It never classifies Gap — so neither does this slide.
slides.why: chapter states 'this is a category-error drift, not a shadow drift' for Tropicana, 'a category error of the highest order' plus 'there is also a shadow reading' for New Coke, and gives Gap no such verdict

slides.title: Customers do not migrate. They stop seeing you.
slides.lead: Three companies. Three archetype drifts. Three rollbacks. The direction of the drift varies; the shape of the failure does not.
bullets: **Tropicana, 2009.** The orange-with-a-straw became a glossy glass of poured juice — the visual language of a Lover or a Ruler, not an Innocent. Within two months sales dropped 20 percent and the company reported losses of more than $30 million in revenue. Regular buyers walked past the new cartons without seeing them.

**Gap, 2010.** Within 24 hours a fashion blog had collected more than 2,000 negative comments. Six days after launch, Gap announced the rollback. *The speed of the rejection is diagnostic* — customers did not need to be convinced.
**New Coke, 1985.** More than 400,000 letters and calls within weeks. Protest groups. A senator entering a statement into the Congressional Record.
The recognition asset is built by the archetype's *specific expression*, not by its name. You cannot swap expressions without losing what accumulated in the original form.

slides.title: New Coke: a commitment made before the real evidence
slides.lead: In blind tests it performed well. Coca-Cola announced the change in April 1985 and discontinued the original formula the same day. Then the actual evidence arrived.
slides.why: chapter narrates a commitment registered on blind-test evidence and resolved by the market months later — 'within three months, Coca-Cola brought back the original formula as Coca-Cola Classic'

marks.label: a statement enters the Congressional Record

slides.title: Five inputs, one conclusion
slides.lead: Ignore what the brand says its archetype is. Read what its behaviour commits to.
slides.why: chapter gives the procedure as five named inputs converging on one name — 'name the archetype that accounts for all five. If you cannot reconcile all five … you have found either a genuine hybrid or evidence of drift in progress'

slides.title: If LinkedIn fails, this is the shape it fails in
slides.lead: Name the archetype, name the shadow, name the early signals — then register the prediction before you have the answer.
slides.why: the chapter registers the claim explicitly and refuses to resolve it: 'the prediction is not that the shadow will activate … whether LinkedIn is currently activating its shadow is a question you can evaluate yourself'

marks.label: signal: tone shifts toward the prescriptive
signal: authority signalling over genuine insight
signal: product rewards performance of expertise

slides.title: Three tests, and you have to survive all of them
slides.lead: You are not choosing a personality. You are choosing a set of constraints you are willing to maintain for years under pressure.
slides.why: chapter names three tests and says 'the archetype that survives all three tests is the one to commit to' — and no verdict is knowable until the reader runs it on their own brand

gates.label: Authenticity
gates.rule: does it match how you behave when you are not performing?

gates.label: Differentiation
gates.rule: or are you one more Sage in a market full of Sages?

gates.label: Stress
gates.rule: does it hold at ten times the size, against a better-funded copy?

slides.title: This is *a* taxonomy, not *the* taxonomy
slides.lead: I should be honest about what this framework cannot do.
bullets: Mark and Pearson is a working decision — concrete enough to teach, general enough to apply across industries, with enough documented case history to defend in a portfolio review. It is not a claim about the deep structure of brand identity.
Real brands combine archetypes. Apple has operated as an Outlaw ("Think Different"), a Magician (the iPhone launch), and arguably a Ruler (the App Store era).

**What would change my mind:** strong evidence that brands without explicit archetype commitments perform comparably, controlling for product quality and marketing spend. The empirical base here is primarily case study.
**Still puzzling:** how brands successfully *evolve* an archetype without losing the audience. I do not have a clean account of it, and I would not trust anyone who claims they do.

slides.section: what this deck does not tell you
slides.title: The stated figures are theirs. The empty slots are yours.
slides.lead: Every number on the drift slides is one the chapter states: 20 percent, $30 million, 2,000 comments, six days, 400,000 letters. Nothing was rounded up to sound better.
bullets: How Gap's failure classifies — shadow drift or category error — **TO RUN**. The chapter analyses the case without assigning it, so this deck leaves the cell dashed rather than filling it with a plausible guess.
Whether LinkedIn's shadow is currently activating — **TO RUN**. Five minutes of the feed, read with this frame, is the experiment.
Whether your candidate archetype survives authenticity, differentiation and stress — **TO RUN**, and only you can run it. The model can name the shadow. Only you know which triggers actually apply.

slides.title: Commit to one identity, then write down how it will fail.
slides.lead: Paste five samples of writing you did without performing a persona and find out which archetype you actually are. Then name your shadow, list three early-warning behaviours specific to you, and set one monthly check. The archetype is the easy half.
